name: Tomato
plantingDepth: 1/4 inch deep for seeds, or plant transplants deep enough to cover the first set of true leaves.
description: A popular warm-season crop that loves heat and needs support. Varieties can be determinate (bush-like) or indeterminate (vining).
tips: Stake or cage indeterminate varieties for support. Water deeply and consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot and foliage diseases. Provide good air circulation to prevent fungal issues. For determinate types, a cage is sufficient. For indeterminate types, use a tall, sturdy stake or cage and tie the main stem to it as it grows.
pruning: For indeterminate varieties, remove 'suckers' (small shoots that form in the 'V' between the main stem and a branch) to encourage larger fruit and better air circulation. Let 1-2 suckers below the first flower cluster grow to increase yield. Determinate varieties do not require pruning.
succession: For indeterminate varieties, one planting is sufficient for a season-long harvest. For determinate (bush) types, plant a second crop 3-4 weeks after the first for a more continuous harvest window.
yield: Varies by type: 5-10 lbs for determinate, 10-30 lbs for indeterminate per plant.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when the fruit is fully colored and firm, but with a slight give. Gently twist the fruit until it detaches from the vine, or use pruners. For green tomatoes, harvest at full size before the first frost and ripen indoors.
containerGardening: Determinate or 'patio' varieties are best. Use a large pot (at least 5-10 gallons) with good drainage and a cage for support. Requires consistent watering as containers dry out fast.

soil.type: Well-drained, loamy soil rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which cause lush foliage but few fruits. Benefits from added calcium (e.g., crushed eggshells) to prevent blossom-end rot.

temperature.notes: A warm-season crop. Fruit will not set at temperatures consistently below 55°F or above 90°F.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store fresh tomatoes at room temperature on the counter, not in the refrigerator, which makes them mealy. For long-term preservation, tomatoes are excellent for canning (whole, diced, or as sauce), freezing (raw or cooked), or drying.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over 7-10 days to prevent transplant shock.

careTasks.name: Install stake or cage at transplant
careTasks.description: Set up support systems early to avoid damaging roots later. As the plant grows, tie stems loosely to the support.

careTasks.name: Prune suckers (indeterminate types)
careTasks.description: Remove small shoots (suckers) that grow in the 'V' between the main stem and branches to improve air circulation and focus energy on fruit.

careTasks.name: Fertilize with low-nitrogen food
careTasks.description: Once fruit begins to set, feed with a fertilizer high in phosphorus and potassium to support fruit development, not excessive leaf growth.

careTasks.name: Check for ripe fruit
careTasks.description: Harvest tomatoes when they are fully colored and firm. Gently twist to remove from the vine.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water deeply to encourage a strong root system, as this helps prevent blossom-end rot. Check moisture by sticking your finger one inch into the soil; if it's dry, it's time to water. Water the base of the plant to keep foliage dry and prevent disease.

name: Bell Pepper
description: A long-season, warm-weather crop that produces sweet, blocky fruits. Part of the nightshade family along with tomatoes and eggplant.
tips: Wait for consistently warm weather and soil. Mulch to retain soil heat and moisture. High heat can cause flower drop. Peppers can be harvested green or left to ripen to red, yellow, or orange for a sweeter flavor and higher vitamin C content.
succession: Not typically needed due to continuous harvesting, but starting a few extra plants can be a buffer against losses. A second planting can extend the harvest in long-season climates.
yield: 5-10+ peppers per plant, depending on variety and conditions.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when fruits reach desired size. Can be picked green and immature, or left on the plant to ripen to its mature color (red, yellow, orange) for a sweeter flavor. Cut the stem with pruners to avoid damaging the plant.
containerGardening: Grows well in 3-5 gallon pots. Ensure good drainage and provide support with a small stake or cage. Potted plants require more frequent watering.

soil.notes: Prefers soil rich in organic matter. A dose of Epsom salts (magnesium sulfate) can help if leaves are yellowing.

temperature.notes: Loves heat. Fruit set can be poor in cool temperatures (below 60°F) or extreme heat (above 90°F).

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store unwashed peppers in the refrigerator's crisper drawer for 1-2 weeks. For long-term storage, peppers can be sliced or diced and frozen raw, or roasted and then frozen.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Apply mulch
careTasks.description: Apply a layer of organic mulch to conserve water, suppress weeds, and keep the soil warm.

careTasks.name: Fertilize when first flowers appear
careTasks.description: Feed with a balanced, low-nitrogen fertilizer to support fruit production.

careTasks.name: Harvest peppers
careTasks.description: Harvest peppers by cutting the stem with scissors or pruners. Pulling can damage the plant. Regular harvesting encourages more fruit set.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Aim for consistent moisture to produce thick-walled, juicy peppers. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry. Mulch helps retain moisture and keep the soil cool.

name: Zucchini
description: An incredibly productive warm-season summer squash. Its rampant growth means a few plants go a long way.
tips: Give it lots of space to sprawl. Harvest fruits when they are small and tender (6-8 inches) for the best flavor. Check under large leaves daily during peak season.
succession: Plant a second crop 3-4 weeks after the first to ensure a supply if squash vine borers or powdery mildew damage the first planting.
yield: Highly productive; 6-10 lbs of fruit per plant is common.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when fruits are 6-8 inches long for best flavor and texture. Skin should be tender and glossy. Check plants daily as they grow quickly. Cut the stem with a knife.
containerGardening: Bush varieties can be grown in large containers (at least 5-10 gallons) with a trellis for support. Requires consistent watering.

soil.notes: Heavy feeder. Amend soil with plenty of compost or aged manure before planting.

temperature.notes: Warm-season crop, very sensitive to frost. Production slows in intense heat.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store unwashed zucchini in a perforated plastic bag in the refrigerator for 5-7 days. For long-term storage, it can be shredded and frozen for use in breads and soups, or blanched and frozen in slices.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Monitor for squash vine borer
careTasks.description: Inspect the base of the stem for small, brown eggs or signs of entry (a hole with 'frass'). Remove eggs and consider wrapping the stem base with foil.

careTasks.name: Check for powdery mildew
careTasks.description: Inspect leaves for white, powdery spots. Improve air circulation by pruning some leaves if necessary. Water at the soil level.

careTasks.name: Harvest fruit regularly
careTasks.description: Harvest zucchini when 6-8 inches long for best flavor and texture. Regular harvesting is key to continuous production.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Provide deep, consistent watering to fuel rapid growth. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry. Aim for the base of the plant to prevent powdery mildew on the leaves.

name: Cucumber
description: A vining plant that needs warm weather and consistent moisture to produce crisp, refreshing fruit. Can be grown on the ground or on a trellis.
tips: Grow on a trellis to save space, improve air circulation, and produce straighter, cleaner fruit. Inconsistent watering can lead to bitter-tasting cucumbers.
succession: Sow seeds every 3-4 weeks for a continuous supply throughout the summer, ensuring a harvest even if early plants succumb to pests or disease.
yield: 10-20 cucumbers per plant, depending on variety (slicing or pickling).
harvestInstructions: Pickling cucumbers are ready at 3-4 inches; slicing cucumbers at 6-8 inches. Harvest regularly to encourage more fruit. Yellowing at the blossom end indicates over-ripeness. Cut the stem with pruners.
containerGardening: Compact or bush varieties are ideal. Use a large pot (5+ gallons) with a trellis. Container-grown cucumbers need frequent watering.

soil.type: Fertile, well-drained soil with lots of organic matter.
soil.notes: Cucumbers are heavy feeders. Side-dress with compost or a balanced fertilizer when vines begin to run.

temperature.notes: Loves warm weather. Growth is stunted by cool temperatures and plants are very frost-sensitive.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store unwashed cucumbers in the refrigerator for up to a week. For long-term preservation, they are ideal for pickling (both as spears and relish) but do not freeze well raw.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Set up trellis
careTasks.description: Install a trellis at planting time. Gently guide vines onto the trellis as they grow.

careTasks.name: Fertilize when vines develop
careTasks.description: Feed with a balanced liquid fertilizer to support vigorous growth and fruit production.

careTasks.name: Harvest cucumbers regularly
careTasks.description: Harvest for pickling when small (3-4 inches) and for slicing at 6-8 inches. Regular picking encourages more fruit.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Inconsistent watering leads to bitter cucumbers. Water deeply whenever the top inch of soil feels dry. Using a trellis and watering at the base helps prevent common leaf diseases.

name: Strawberry (June-Bearing)
plantingDepth: Plant with the crown (where leaves emerge) exactly at soil level. Do not bury the crown or it will rot.
wateringNeeds: Consistent moisture, especially during fruit development
description: A low-growing perennial fruit that establishes in year one and produces a large, concentrated crop for a few weeks in late spring or early summer of year two.
tips: Pinch off all flowers in the first year to encourage a strong root system and more runners. Mulch with straw to keep berries clean and suppress weeds.
succession: Not applicable in the traditional sense. For a longer harvest season, plant a mix of June-bearing, everbearing, and day-neutral varieties to cover different harvest windows.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when berries are fully and uniformly red, as they will not ripen further after picking. Pick in the cool of the morning. Grasp the stem just above the berry and pinch it off.
containerGardening: Excellent for containers, hanging baskets, and strawberry pots. Ensure good drainage. Everbearing and day-neutral types are often preferred for containers due to a longer, smaller harvest.

soil.type: Well-drained, sandy loam with high organic matter.
soil.notes: Prefers slightly acidic soil. Avoid planting where tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant were previously grown to avoid verticillium wilt.

temperature.notes: Plants are very frost-hardy, but blossoms are sensitive to late spring frosts. Cover if frost is predicted.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover blossoms to protect fruit production from frost.

storage: Refrigerate unwashed berries in a single layer for 2-3 days. Wash just before eating. For long-term storage, strawberries freeze beautifully (whole or sliced) and are perfect for making jam.

careTasks.name: Pinch off all flowers (First Year)
careTasks.description: For the entire first season, remove any flowers that appear. This directs the plant's energy into developing a robust root system and healthy runners.

careTasks.name: Apply mulch
careTasks.description: Apply a thick layer of straw mulch around plants to keep berries off the soil, conserve moisture, and control weeds.

careTasks.name: Harvest berries (Year 2+)
careTasks.description: Harvest when berries are fully red. Pick every couple of days as they ripen quickly.

careTasks.name: Renovate bed after harvest (Year 2+)
careTasks.description: After harvest is complete, mow the leaves, narrow the rows, remove weeds, and fertilize to prepare for the next season.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Strawberries have shallow roots and require consistent water, especially during fruit development. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry. Mulching with straw helps keep soil moist and berries clean.

name: Pumpkin
description: A vining, warm-season crop that requires a lot of space and a long growing season to produce its iconic fall fruit.
tips: Water at the base of the plant to prevent powdery mildew. Place a board or straw under developing fruits to prevent rot from contact with wet soil.
succession: Not applicable due to the long season and space requirements. Plant different varieties for different sizes and uses.
yield: 2-5 pumpkins per plant, depending on variety.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when the pumpkin has reached its mature color and the rind is hard. A hollow sound when thumped is a good indicator. Leave 3-4 inches of stem attached to the pumpkin, as this 'handle' helps it store longer. Cure in the sun for 7-10 days before storing.
containerGardening: Not recommended for most varieties due to sprawling vines and large fruit size. Miniature varieties may be grown in very large (20+ gallon) containers with strong trellising.

soil.notes: Very heavy feeder. Mix in generous amounts of compost or aged manure into the planting hill.

temperature.notes: Requires a long, warm growing season. Very sensitive to frost.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: After curing, store in a cool, dry place (50-55°F) with good air circulation for 2-3 months. For culinary use, pumpkin puree can be frozen for up to a year.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings to 2-3 per mound
careTasks.description: Remove weaker seedlings to ensure the strongest plants have adequate space and resources.

careTasks.name: Monitor for squash vine borer
careTasks.description: Inspect the base of the plant for small, brown eggs and signs of entry. Take preventive action if found.

careTasks.name: Fertilize when vines begin to run
careTasks.description: Feed with a low-nitrogen, high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage flowering and fruit set.

careTasks.name: Elevate developing fruit
careTasks.description: Place a piece of cardboard, a board, or straw under each pumpkin to keep it dry and prevent rot.

careTasks.name: Harvest before first hard frost
careTasks.description: Harvest when the pumpkin is a deep, uniform color and the rind is hard. Leave 3-4 inches of stem attached.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: The goal is to water deeply and infrequently to encourage strong root growth. Water when the top 1-2 inches of soil feel dry. Reduce watering as pumpkins mature to promote curing.

name: Eggplant
description: A heat-loving, warm-season crop that produces beautiful, glossy fruit. A staple in many cuisines.
tips: Wait for consistently warm weather (day and night) before transplanting. Harvest when skin is glossy and firm. Overripe fruits become seedy and bitter.
succession: Not typically needed, as plants produce continuously until frost if harvested regularly.
yield: 4-8 fruits per plant, depending on variety.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when fruits have reached a good size, their skin is glossy, and they are firm to the touch. If you press the skin and it leaves an indent, it's ripe. If it's hard, it's immature. If it's soft and dull, it's overripe. Cut with pruners, leaving a small piece of stem.
containerGardening: Compact varieties grow well in 5-gallon or larger pots. They need consistent water and support or staking as fruit develops.

soil.notes: Heavy feeder. Amend soil with compost. Benefits from regular feeding throughout the season.

temperature.notes: Thrives in heat. Production will be poor if temperatures are too cool, especially at night.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store in the crisper drawer of the refrigerator for 5-7 days. For longer storage, eggplant can be blanched and frozen, or cooked into dishes like ratatouille and then frozen.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Stake or cage plants
careTasks.description: Provide support before the plant is heavy with fruit to prevent stems from breaking.

careTasks.name: Fertilize when first fruits set
careTasks.description: Feed with a balanced liquid fertilizer to support healthy growth and continued fruit development.

careTasks.name: Monitor for flea beetles
careTasks.description: Check leaves for tiny holes, a sign of flea beetles. Use row covers on young plants for protection.

careTasks.name: Harvest fruit
careTasks.description: Harvest when fruits have reached a good size, their skin is glossy, and they are firm to the touch. Cut the stem with pruners.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Eggplant requires consistent moisture for the best quality fruit. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry. Mulching helps retain soil moisture and suppress weeds.

name: Winter Squash (Butternut)
description: A vining, warm-season crop that produces hard-skinned squash that can be stored for months.
tips: Harvest when the rind is hard and cannot be easily dented with a fingernail. Leave a few inches of stem attached. Cure in the sun for 10 days before storing.
succession: Not applicable due to long growing season. Plant different winter squash varieties for a diverse winter pantry.
harvestInstructions: Harvest before the first hard frost, when the squash has turned a solid tan color and the rind is too hard to be pierced with a fingernail. Leave at least 2 inches of stem attached. Cure in a sunny spot for 1-2 weeks before storing.
containerGardening: Bush or compact vining types can be grown in very large containers (10-20 gallons) with strong trellising, but it can be challenging.

soil.notes: Heavy feeder. Amend planting hills with generous amounts of compost or aged manure.

temperature.notes: Requires a long, warm growing season. Very sensitive to frost.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: After curing, store in a cool, dry, dark place with good air circulation (50-60°F) for 3-6 months. Cooked, pureed squash freezes very well.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Monitor for squash bugs and vine borers
careTasks.description: Check leaves for squash bug eggs and the base of stems for vine borer damage.

careTasks.name: Elevate developing fruit
careTasks.description: Place a piece of cardboard, a board, or straw under each squash to keep it from direct contact with moist soil, preventing rot.

careTasks.name: Harvest before first hard frost
careTasks.description: Harvest when squash has turned a deep, solid tan color and the rind is hard. Leave 2-3 inches of stem attached.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Winter squash needs deep, infrequent watering to develop strong roots. Water when the top 1-2 inches of soil feel dry. Taper off watering as the fruit cures on the vine.

name: Watermelon
wateringNeeds: Deep, consistent watering until fruit sets
description: A sprawling, warm-season crop that needs a long, hot growing season to produce large, sweet fruit.
tips: Reduce watering as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Look for multiple signs of ripeness: the tendril closest to the fruit stem is dry and brown, the spot where it rests on the ground is yellow, and it sounds hollow when thumped.
succession: Not applicable due to long growing season and large space requirements. For different harvest times, choose varieties with different days-to-maturity.
harvestInstructions: Check for three signs of ripeness: 1) The tendril closest to the melon stem is dry and brown. 2) The spot where the melon rests on the ground (the 'belly') has turned from white to a creamy yellow. 3) The melon sounds deep and hollow when thumped.
containerGardening: Smaller 'icebox' varieties can be grown in large (10-20 gallon) containers with a strong trellis. Requires very consistent watering.

soil.notes: Heavy feeder. Amend soil with compost and a balanced fertilizer.

temperature.notes: Needs heat to thrive and develop sugars. Very frost sensitive.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Uncut melons can be stored in a cool place for a week or two. Once cut, wrap tightly and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Flesh can be pureed and frozen for slushies or sorbets.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Elevate developing melons
careTasks.description: Place cardboard, straw, or a board under developing fruit to prevent rot and insect damage.

careTasks.name: Reduce watering for sweetness
careTasks.description: Once melons have reached full size, reduce watering to allow sugars to concentrate in the fruit.

careTasks.name: Check for ripeness
careTasks.description: Check the ground spot (should be yellow), the tendril nearest the stem (should be dry), and the sound when thumped (should be hollow).

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water deeply and consistently to produce sweet, juicy melons. Check moisture by sticking your finger 1-2 inches into the soil. Reduce watering as melons ripen to concentrate their sweetness.

name: Cantaloupe
wateringNeeds: Consistent moisture until fruit sets, then reduce
description: A warm-season vine crop that produces fragrant, sweet melons with a netted skin.
tips: A ripe cantaloupe will slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure and have a sweet, musky aroma at the blossom end.
succession: In long-season areas, a second planting can be made 3-4 weeks after the first for a later harvest.
harvestInstructions: Ripe cantaloupes will have a fragrant, musky aroma at the blossom end and the melon should 'slip' from the vine with gentle pressure at the stem. The netting on the skin will be pronounced and the color underneath should be tan or yellow, not green.
containerGardening: Compact or bush varieties are suitable for large (5-10 gallon) containers with trellising. Consistent watering is crucial.

soil.notes: Heavy feeder. Amend soil with compost and feed regularly with a balanced fertilizer.

temperature.notes: Needs heat to develop sugars. Very frost sensitive.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store uncut melons at room temperature for a few days or in the fridge for up to a week. Once cut, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Flesh can be frozen.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Monitor for powdery mildew
careTasks.description: Inspect leaves for white, powdery spots. Ensure good air circulation and water at the soil level.

careTasks.name: Reduce watering for sweetness
careTasks.description: Once melons have reached their full size, reduce watering to concentrate sugars in the fruit.

careTasks.name: Check for ripeness (slip test)
careTasks.description: Check for a crack forming at the stem attachment point. A ripe melon will detach ('slip') from the vine with very little effort.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Provide consistent water for the sweetest melons. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry. Reduce watering as the melon ripens and develops its netted skin.

name: Okra
description: A heat-loving, warm-season crop that produces edible green pods and beautiful, hibiscus-like flowers.
tips: Harvest pods when they are young and tender (3-4 inches long). Wear gloves when harvesting, as some varieties have spines that can irritate the skin.
succession: Not necessary. Plants will produce continuously until the first frost if pods are picked regularly.
yield: 20-30+ pods per plant over the season.
harvestInstructions: Harvest pods when they are 2-4 inches long and tender. Pick every 1-2 days to encourage continuous production. Use pruners or a knife. Pods become woody and tough if left on the plant too long.
containerGardening: Dwarf varieties are well-suited for 5-gallon pots. Okra has a deep taproot, so use a deep container. Loves heat and sun.

soil.notes: Tolerant of various soil types but thrives with compost amendment. Does not need heavy feeding.

temperature.notes: Thrives in heat and humidity. Wait for soil to be thoroughly warm before planting.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Best used fresh. Store dry and unwashed in a paper bag in the warmest part of the refrigerator for 2-3 days. For long-term storage, okra can be blanched and frozen (whole or sliced), pickled, or dried.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Fertilize when pods form
careTasks.description: Side-dress with compost or a balanced fertilizer to support the long production season.

careTasks.name: Harvest pods every 1-2 days
careTasks.description: Harvest pods when they are 3-4 inches long. If they get too large, they become tough. Frequent picking is essential for continuous production.

careTasks.name: Monitor for aphids
careTasks.description: Check new growth and the undersides of leaves for aphids. A strong spray of water can dislodge them.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Okra is drought-tolerant but produces best with consistent moisture. Water deeply when the top 1-2 inches of soil feel dry, especially during hot, dry spells.

name: Rhubarb
plantingDepth: Plant crowns so the top is 1-2 inches below the soil surface.
wateringNeeds: Deep watering, especially in dry spells
description: A perennial vegetable most often treated as a fruit. Known for its tart, edible stalks and very large leaves. Extremely cold hardy and long-lived.
tips: Never eat the leaves - they contain high levels of oxalic acid and are toxic. Harvest stalks by pulling and twisting at the base, not cutting.
succession: Not applicable. A well-cared-for perennial plant will produce for 10+ years.
yield: 2-4 lbs of stalks per mature plant per season.
harvestInstructions: Do not harvest in the first year. In year two, take a light harvest. From year three on, harvest stalks that are at least 10-12 inches long by firmly grasping the stalk near the base and pulling with a twisting motion. Never eat the leaves.
containerGardening: Can be grown in a very large (20+ gallon) container, but requires a cold winter dormancy period, which can be difficult to achieve in a pot. Not ideal for container gardening long-term.

soil.type: Deep, well-drained soil, rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Heavy feeder. Top-dress with a thick layer of compost or aged manure each spring.

temperature.notes: Requires a dormant period with temperatures below 40°F to stimulate spring growth. Dislikes intense summer heat.

environmentalAlerts.message: Rhubarb is very cold hardy, but a hard freeze can damage stalks. Cover if a hard freeze is expected.

storage: Refrigerate unwashed stalks in a plastic bag for up to two weeks. For long-term storage, chop stalks and freeze them raw, or cook them down into a sauce before freezing.

careTasks.name: Do not harvest (First Year)
careTasks.description: Do not harvest any stalks in the first year to allow the plant to establish a strong root system.

careTasks.name: Remove flower stalks
careTasks.description: Cut any large, round flower stalks that appear as soon as you see them. This directs the plant's energy into leaf and stalk growth.

careTasks.name: Begin light harvest (Year 2)
careTasks.description: Harvest a few of the thickest stalks for about 4 weeks. Leave at least two-thirds of the stalks on the plant.

careTasks.name: Full harvest (Year 3+)
careTasks.description: Harvest stalks for 8-10 weeks, but stop by mid-summer to allow the plant to store energy for next year. Never take more than half the stalks at once.

careTasks.name: Divide crowns every 5-7 years
careTasks.description: In early spring or fall, dig up and divide large crowns to reinvigorate the plant and create new ones.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Rhubarb thrives with consistent moisture which helps produce tender stalks. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, especially during hot, dry summer periods.
